About .NET installations Top About .NET installations The .NET framework, in addition to making across the Web inter-operability simpler and easier also provides the a number of advantages when it comes to deploying and maintaining applications when compared to conventional software in the past.

Title: How to set up About .NET installations
Steps:
About .NET installations Top About .NET installations The .NET framework, in addition to making across the Web inter-operability simpler and easier also provides the a number of advantages when it comes to deploying and maintaining applications when compared to conventional software in the past. Advantages of .NET installations over conventional software installations: - In the past one of the greatest headache with installing (deploying) applications, were shared DLLs (dynamic-link libraries), which has been termed "DLL Hell" for the following reasons: - Firstly, these files needed to be dispersed across hard disk in common folders, such as System32. This both complicated the process of backing up and removing these applications and caused the hard drive to become cluttered with these files. - Secondly, these files could easily be overwritten by newer versions that were not backward compatible with the version already on the computer. Which could cause one or more of the existing applications to either work incorrectly or stop working completely. .NET applications, however, prevent potential conflicts between applications by isolating their assemblies formerly known as a dynamic linked libraries (.DLL files), which is externally compiled and contains a collection of properties or methods that can be implemented within a script. in their individual installation folders. For this reason, multiple versions of an assembly can be installed and run simultaneously on the same computer. Furthermore .NET applications record the version information of its component assemblies and verify these versions before it is run. Any version differences detected prevent the application from running and display an appropriate warning instead. Therefore .NET applications always load the components with which they were built and tested. - In the past applications were forced to use the registry to store their user-configurable settings and any other application-specific information, which in many cases complicated the process of replicating and backing up these applications effectively. .NET applications are no longer tied to using the registry to save its user-customizable settings. Instead these settings are saved in .CONFIG files (a type of .INI file), which reside within the application’s installation folder and can be opened and edited in any text editor. In short by making .NET applications entirely self-contained the major hiccups that previously complicating the process of installing, copying, backing up and removing conventional software, have been removed. This means that the installation folder of a .NET application now contains: - All of its dependent assemblies formerly known as a dynamic linked libraries (.DLL files), which is externally compiled and contains a collection of properties or methods that can be implemented within a script. , with each assembly having the specific version that this application was built and tested with. - All the user-customizable settings for the application, contained within its .CONFIG file This .NET file is similar to an .INI file, in a single .CONFIG file is used per application to contain its user-configurable settings. This text file is located in the installation folder and has the same name as its application. . Although this does mean that it is no longer essential to install a .NET application, an installation is still preferred, since it does still makes it easier to manage the copied files and to perform any further configuration, such as the setting up of services etc. Note: If you do not install the product, then you will need to run the .NET framework’s InitExe application to install the required .NET services, yourself. -->

About Adroit Backup Utility Top About Adroit Backup Utility How to Use this Adroit Backup Utility The Adroit Backup Utility makes it possible to create a complete backup of your Adroit installation.

Title: About Adroit Backup Utility
Steps:
About Adroit Backup Utility Top About Adroit Backup Utility How to Use this Adroit Backup Utility The Adroit Backup Utility makes it possible to create a complete backup of your Adroit installation. This should be used to protect your Adroit installation from corruption or possible accidental deletion and also provides an easy way for transferring an Adroit project or system to another computer. This consists of the following 4 sections, which can be enabled or disabled according to your needs: - Adroit installation files : backs up the files required by the Adroit application. - Adroit data files : backs up the files required by your Adroit projects, where multiple file locations can be specified. - Event Logs : ONLY exports the application; security and system event logs files. These event log files CANNOT be restored but can be viewed. - Adroit registry : backs up both the global Adroit registry settings and the Adroit registry settings specific to the current user. Once the back up has been appropriately configured, click the Backup now button to execute the back up. The Backup path , allows you to specify where these Adroit backups are to be stored . The Overwrite option determines if previous backups are preserved or overwritten , affecting the structure of the saved backup directory . The Adroit Backup Utility makes use of profiles to store different backup configuration settings for later reuse and as these profiles can be executed from the command-line , Adroit backups are also able to be scheduled or run from a batch file. The Set defaults button can be used to save the configured backup settings as the Default profile settings, this is recommended if the current settings are to be frequently used. On exit the currently configured settings are saved to the currently selected profile . -->

About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) Top About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) The Agent Server is a collection or container of the supported agent types and stores and manages the instances of their created agents, by providing consistent mechanisms for creating and destroying agents and accessing the information contained within them.

Title: About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage)
About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) Top About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) The Agent Server is a collection or container of the supported agent types and stores and manages the instances of their created agents, by providing consistent mechanisms for creating and destroying agents and accessing the information contained within them. Each agent type is a Windows Dynamic Link Library (.DLL) file in the Adroit system folder, which is loaded when the Agent Server starts up, making its functionality available for use. The Adroit database (.WGP) file or load file stores almost all of the data and configuration of the Agent Server. This includes every agent that has been added to the current project of this Agent Server, with the exception of the agents that are automatically created or dynamic agents like Proxy and Scan agents. Note: For this reason it essential that this Adroit database (.WGP) file is frequently backed up. For details, see Backing Up Adroit Database (.WGP) Files . This ASCII text file is associated with a specific project and is loaded when the Agent Server starts up. For further details concerning projects, see About Adroit Projects . However, the only component of Adroit that knows anything about the meaning of data stored for each agent in this Adroit database, is the agent type (.DLL) file. Therefore, this Adroit database (.WGP) file or load file is only loaded once all the agent type (.DLL) files have been loaded by the Agent Server. For details of the format of each agent type when an agent is saved to the Adroit database (.WGP) file, see Agent Type Saved Format Reference . Note: If it becomes necessary to edit this file manually, you must ensure that a Carriage Return terminates the last line of the .WGP file. The Agent Server will look for following two load files when it starts up: - The .WGP load file for the required project that is specified by the Auto-Load Filename field in the Agent Server Configuration page of the Adroit Configuration Utility. - When this has been successfully loaded, the Agent Server will look for a second (optional) file called POSTLOAD.WGP, which creates and configures the default agents. For details, see Postload Adroit Database File . Note : Further agents can be loaded from other .WGP files whenever the user wishes. For details, see Methods of Creating Agents . In Adroit , an Agent Server can also be configured as a cluster server, which is a set of two servers running a replicated database (WGP file) on the same project. For details, see Active Clusters Foundation . -->

About Adroit Projects Top About Adroit Projects A project in Adroit , is the default mechanism for allowing multiple distributed Agent Servers to seamlessly share their agents and the data that they contain.

Title: About Adroit Projects
About Adroit Projects Top About Adroit Projects A project in Adroit , is the default mechanism for allowing multiple distributed Agent Servers to seamlessly share their agents and the data that they contain. In other words, if Agent Server A and Agent Server B have the SAME project name (and are in the same network domain), then Agent Server A is able to refer to agents within Agent Server B and vice verse. For further details of how Adroit projects work and their limitations and the other mechanisms that are provided to overcome these limitations, see Agent Server Connection Methods . Note: Proxy agents are automatically created when an Agent Server accesses an agent that exists in a remote Agent Server. This provides client applications with a transparent mechanism for accessing agents, so that a distributed agent database acts as a standalone database. In other words, even though a Classic UI connects to a single Agent Server, one or its mimics or pictures can display agents that exist on a remote Agent Server. All Agent Servers need to specify a project name whether they are standalone (a single Agent Server on one computer) or distributed (requiring more than one Agent Server). While it is essential that each Agent Server has a unique name, project names should only be the same for those Agent Server that are required to communicate to one another. Configure the required Project and Agent Server name in the Agent Server Configuration page of the Adroit Configuration utility. A number of other configuration requirements must be met before a distributed project can be created. For details, see Requirements for Distributed Agent Servers. Tip: According to the best practices the Adroit Software should always be separated from the configured project(s), for this reason, a directory for Adroit projects should be created. For details, see Best Practices . Note: It is important to create a backup procedure to guarantee disaster avoidance rather than just disaster recovery and also to provide an easy way for transferring an Adroit project or system to another computer. For details, see About Backup Procedures . -->

About Agent Data (Slots) Top About Agent Data (Slots) Each agent (instance of an agent type) maintains its own unique set of data and is referred to by its own unique agent name.

Title: About Agent Data (Slots)
About Agent Data (Slots) Top About Agent Data (Slots) Each agent (instance of an agent type) maintains its own unique set of data and is referred to by its own unique agent name. For details, see About Agents or Naming Agents . Most agents are designed to contain multiple items of data, which are referred to as agent attributes. Most of these attributes are accessible to clients of the Agent Server as slots of the agent. Slots can therefore be defined as externally accessible attributes of an agent. For details, see Accessing Agent Slots . For instance, the Analog agent slot has a hiHi slot that allows a value to be assigned that represents the high-high alarm limit for an analog signal. There are clearly different types of data that need to be stored in an agent. For example, the name, is an ASCII string, whereas the hiHi limit, referred to above, is a floating point Real number value, and the state of a Digital is a Boolean TRUE/FALSE indication. This implies the concept of slot type , as well as agent type. For details, see Slot Types . An Adroit configuration is therefore made of many different agents, each of which is a unique instance of one of the supported agent types. Each agent, in turn, contains externally accessible data attributes, or slots, whose type corresponds to one of the supported slot types. For details of the available slots for each agent type, see Agent Type Slot Reference . An agent's "state", at any instant in time, is defined as the collective values of all its data. Agents have both generic and type-specific data. For details, see Data Structure of an Agent . Note: The overall status of an agent can be determined from its status slot, which is common to all agent types. For details, see Agent Status . -->

About Agent Servers Top About Agent Servers The Agent Server is the storage facility for all real time and historical data.

Title: About Agent Servers
About Agent Servers Top About Agent Servers The Agent Server is the storage facility for all real time and historical data. - The real time data resides within intelligent objects, known as agents, which exchange messages with other agents or picture objects either from their local host computer or from remote computer nodes elsewhere on the network. - Historical data is written to disk where it is available for rapid retrieval and on-line analysis. Note: Redundancy can be provided by configuring the Agent Server as a cluster server, which is a set of two Agent Servers running a replicated database. For details, see About Active Clustering and Important Points to consider when Clustering Agent Servers . Agents are described as intelligent because they store live data as well as providing methods of manipulating that data. Agents can be both clients and servers at the same time, by operating on, and being operated upon, by other agents. For details, see About Agents . The interaction of the agents with each other as well as with the Classic User Interface and its picture objects, provides a powerful and dynamic monitoring and control capability which reflects the status of your process in real-time. For further details, see What you can do in Adroit . Agents are classified by function into a number of agent types, which can be used to implement a wide variety of system related, as well as application-specific tasks. For details, see About Agent Types . Note: An instance of an agent type is usually referred to as an agent. The Agent Server is therefore a collection or container of the supported agent types and stores and manages the instances of their created agents, in an agent database (.WGP) file. For further details regarding the storage of agents, see About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) . Note: The Agent Server is the only component in Adroit that needs to be licensed. For details, see Adroit Licensing . Adroit OEMs, distributors, and even power end-users can create their own custom agent types programmatically by using the Adroit agent interface. However, it is also possible to use the Custom agent type and its associated Custom Agent Designer utility. For details, see How to Use the Custom Agent Designer . Due to the way in which Adroit has been designed, there are no theoretical limits to the number of different agents that can be contained within an Agent Server. In addition, multiple Agent Servers can be distributed across many physical computers, in a local or wide area network, by using the concept of a Project. For this reason, the total number of agents that can exist in an Adroit installation is effectively unlimited. For further details concerning Projects in Adroit , see About Adroit Projects . Furthermore, because 32 bit Windows supports multi-threaded applications, Adroit Agent Servers can concurrently interact with as many client workstations as may be required. This feature is facilitated by Adroit agent level locking which ensures orderly access to any instance of an agent. Adroit provides consistent mechanisms for creating and deleting agents, as well as efficient means of accessing information contained within them, making it easy to manage these agent collections. The Agent Server is typically configured by means of the Configurator dialog in the Classic UI or by means of the Project Explorer. For details, see Configuring the Agent Server or The Project Explorer . Adroit Agent Servers, provide two basic methods of accessing the data within agents: - The first allows a user to get a data value from or put a data value into an agent.

- The second allows a user to register as a subscriber to another agent, and then to be notified whenever the relevant value changes.

Title: About Agent Servers
- The second allows a user to register as a subscriber to another agent, and then to be notified whenever the relevant value changes. These subscriptions make for significant reductions in processor load, since changing values will not be communicated to a subscriber until necessary. Command-line Options for the Agent Server . About Agent Types Top About Agent Types Adroit configurations are composed of intelligent, cooperating objects known as agents .

Title: About Agent Types
About Agent Types Top About Agent Types Adroit configurations are composed of intelligent, cooperating objects known as agents . For details, see About Agents . These agents are differentiated into different types to provide specific information storage and manipulation mechanisms, with their intended function determining their complexity. By default, these agent types are further separated into the following categories to better facilitate the selection of the required agent when designing your system, as follows: - Basic : these agent types form the basic building blocks of a system and are used for gathering, handling and processing data to and from the physical external world. Analog, Counter, Date, Digital, Expression, Marshal, MultiState, String, StringList, Timer - Advanced : these agent types provide powerful SCADA and integration functionality that allow the Basic agents to be alarmed and logged to databases and provides various means of reporting and/or controlling their values. Accumulator, AgentGroup, Alarm, Alarm List, AlarmManagement, ARec, Command, DbAccess, DBLog, EventLogging, EventOutput, Multimedia, Notify, Recipe, Scheduler, Script, Shift, Statistical - MIS/MES : these are very specific and usually quite complex agent types used to do monitor, control and solve higher level shop-floor and general industrial challenges. MaxDemand, OEE, PID - IT : these agent types facilitate the integration and management of SCADA and IT Audit, DumpConfig, ICMP, Perfmon, SNMPMgr - System : these agent types are used internally to perform certain SCADA and other specific functions. Note: Instances of these Agents are created automatically and cannot be added manually by the user. Alias, Beeper, DataLog, Device, Hasp, Proxy, Scan, SystemDataLog, SystemInformation - Primitive : these agent types are primitive because they offer limited value and are limited in functionality when compared to the Basic agents, they are essentially single value containers. Boolean, Integer, Real, Text and Frame IMPORTANT: These agent types CANNOT be alarmed and their values are not scaled etc, so use the Basic agent types instead to represent your process values. For more details about each of these available agent types, see Available Agents . Note: If you are using Adroit in HMI mode, then some of these agent types are NOT available. For details, see HMI Mode . For details about using these default agent groups to limit the available agent types displayed in the Type list of the Agent Configurator dialog, see Selecting default agent groups . Note: It is also possible to change which agent types belong to each of these agent type categories (see Grouping Agents Together ). -->

Analog, Counter, Date, Digital, Expression, Marshal, MultiState, String, StringList, Timer - Advanced : these agent types provide powerful SCADA and integration functionality that allow the Basic agents to be alarmed and logged to databases and provides various means of reporting and/or controlling their values. Accumulator, AgentGroup, Alarm, Alarm List, AlarmManagement, ARec, Command, DbAccess, DBLog, EventLogging, EventOutput, Multimedia, Notify, Recipe, Scheduler, Script, Shift, Statistical - MIS/MES : these are very specific and usually quite complex agent types used to do monitor, control and solve higher level shop-floor and general industrial challenges. MaxDemand, OEE, PID - IT : these agent types facilitate the integration and management of SCADA and IT Audit, DumpConfig, ICMP, Perfmon, SNMPMgr - System : these agent types are used internally to perform certain SCADA and other specific functions. Note: Instances of these Agents are created automatically and cannot be added manually by the user. Alias, Beeper, DataLog, Device, Hasp, Proxy, Scan, SystemDataLog, SystemInformation - Primitive : these agent types are primitive because they offer limited value and are limited in functionality when compared to the Basic agents, they are essentially single value containers. Boolean, Integer, Real, Text and Frame IMPORTANT: These agent types CANNOT be alarmed and their values are not scaled etc, so use the Basic agent types instead to represent your process values. For more details about each of these available agent types, see "Available Agents" on page 1 . Note: If you are using Adroit in HMI mode, then some of these agent types are NOT available. For details, see "HMI Mode" on page 1 . For details about using these default agent groups to limit the available agent types displayed in the Type list of the Agent Configurator dialog, see Selecting default agent groups .

Note: It is also possible to change which agent types belong to each of these agent type categories (see Grouping Agents Together ).

About Agents Top About Agents The Agent Server is the storage facility for all agents.

Title: About Agents
About Agents Top About Agents The Agent Server is the storage facility for all agents. For details, see About Agent Servers . Agents are called agents because, instead of only containing data, like simple database records, they also usually contain the ability to operate or act on their own data, driving its values and to read and write to other objects, and so influence them. This concept is very much in line with object-oriented thinking, and is primarily why we refer to Adroit as being "object-oriented". Note: When referring to a data value within an agent this is often referred to as a tag. For details, see Agents, Slots, Tags and their relation to Values . Agents are classified by function into a number of agent types, which can be used to implement a wide variety of system related, as well as application-specific tasks. For details, see About Agent Types . For example, the Analog agent type is used to handle the signal conditioning and alarm checking requirements of a process variable, and the DataLog agent type is responsible for creating, maintaining, and accessing historical data logs. An agent is therefore, more correctly, an instance of an agent type, for example an instance of the Analog agent type could be the TANKLEVEL Analog agent (assuming that this agent has been created by a user). Each of these agent types have well defined rules for interfacing with other agents ensuring that an extremely robust and versatile environment has been created to handle any real world situation. For this reason each Adroit agent can be dynamically configured to benefit from specific functions provided by other agent types, such as scanning ( Communicating Values ), alarming ( Alarming Values ) and logging ( Logging values ). The interaction of these agents with each other as well as with the Classic User Interface and its picture objects, provides a powerful and dynamic monitoring and control capability which reflects the status of your process in real-time. For each agent type, there may be zero, one or many agent instances. Each time you add an agent, you are creating a new agent instance, however, agent instances are simply referred to as agents. Every agent, with the exception of the agents that are automatically created or dynamic agents like Proxy and Scan agents, are stored in an Adroit database (.WGP) file. For details, see About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) . All agents have three essential characteristics, namely: - Identity: An agent is referred to by its unique name, which is decided by you when creating it. For example, the Analog agent type may have 5 agents created by the user called ANA01, ANA02, RPM, TEMPERATURE_INLET_01 and FEED_TANK_LEVEL. For details, see Naming Agents . - State: The state of an agent is the instantaneous snapshot of all its data values, some of which are externally accessible as slots. For details, see Agent Data or Slots . Note: The overall status of an agent can be determined from its status slot, which is common to all agent types. For details, see Agent Status . - Functionality: The functions and algorithmic procedures within the agent give the agent its functional characteristics. For details, see Agent Functionality . -->

About Alarm Acknowledgement Top About Alarm Acknowledgement Acknowledgment is typically recommended for alarms or incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type.

Title: About Alarm Acknowledgement
About Alarm Acknowledgement Top About Alarm Acknowledgement Acknowledgment is typically recommended for alarms or incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). that require some sort of reaction or attention from the operator. In other words, an alarm should be any event that an operator must understand, acknowledge and respond to – and not simply acknowledge and ignore. Therefore you should carefully consider, which incidents require acknowledgement and which do not. Adroit provides the following methods of acknowledging alarms: - Global acknowledgement: This should be used when using a standalone Adroit installation or for those alarms that only one operator needs to be made aware of. By globally acknowledging an alarm from any computer in the network, this incident will be removed from ALL the lists in the system (provided, of course, that the alarm is no longer active). - Local acknowledgement: This should be used when you have alarms that more that one operator needs to be aware of. Click for more details: In other words you have a distributed Adroit installation, with operators viewing the process from remote user interfaces. Local acknowledge refers to the action of acknowledging an alarm in an alarm list of an AlarmList agent. This removes the alarm from this alarm list, provided the alarm is no longer active. If the alarm is routed to other alarm lists (usually on other computers), locally acknowledging the alarm one alarm list will not clear the alarm from these other alarm lists. This method therefore requires that each operator locally (remotely) acknowledges the alarm, to remove it from their alarm list (once it is no longer active the monitored condition of this incident (alarm/event) is still in effect and has not yet returned to its normal operating state. ). Note1: In the case of local alarm acknowledgement, you need to use the AlarmList agent to contain these incidents and NOT the Alarm agent. For further details of using AlarmLists and displaying alarms, see Displaying Alarms . Note2: Once an incident has been locally (remotely) acknowledged from a remote UI, the color of this alarm changes (to blue by default) so that the other operators can see that this has occurred.

However, each operator that views this alarm still needs to locally acknowledge it before it is removed from the list.

Title: About Alarm Acknowledgement
However, each operator that views this alarm still needs to locally acknowledge it before it is removed from the list. Only when this alarm is globally acknowledged is it removed from the global alarm list of the Alarm agent. For more details about enabling or disabling the acknowledgement of incidents, see Configuring Incident Acknowledgement . For details about acknowledging alarms using the Alarm List Viewer window, see Acknowledging Alarms. Note: To define how the alarming subsystem treats current alarms if an agent’s statusalarmInhibit slot is set to one and the agent is currently in alarm and/or unacknowledged, add and configure the SmartInhibit registry value. If you route incidents to an AlarmManagement agent, then instead of operators simply acknowledging an incident, by pressing a button, you can have them: - specify the reason and sub-reason that caused this incident and/or - specify additional notes relating to this incident. These measures will improve your incident reviews. You can also have your operators launch a HTML document relating specifically to each incident to help them both UNDERSTAND and RESPOND appropriately to this incident. For details of how to use the AlarmManagement agent, see Quick Start to Configure and Record Incidents (Alarms/Events) . For details about hiding or showing the local and/or global acknowledgement buttons of the Alarm List Viewer window, see Securing Acknowledge Buttons in Alarm Windows. -->

About Alarm Management Top About Alarm Management Alarm management is concerned with improving the QUALITY of the information within the alarming configuration.

Title: About Alarm Management
Steps:
About Alarm Management Top About Alarm Management Alarm management is concerned with improving the QUALITY of the information within the alarming configuration. This information should be used to reduce the QUANTITY of nuisance alarms (red herrings) so that only the most important and relevant alarms are displayed for your process. In other words, alarm management can counteract inefficient alarming. Up to now SCADA installations have used numerous alarms, each of which usually have very little awareness of the other alarms in the system. So generally each incident generates a flood of alarms, which operators simply ignore because there are too many to deal with. According to the EEMUA 191 guidelines a document created by the Engineering Equipment & Materials Users' Association ( EEMUA) of alarm management guidelines, developed by the users of alarm systems, and is the globally accepted and leading guide to good practice for alarm management. : - An alarm is an incident that an operator must understand, acknowledge and respond to – not simply acknowledge and ignore. For further details, see Effective Alarm Characteristics . - No process should have more than 6 such alarm occurrences an hour during normal operations. - Under abnormal process conditions no more than 10 alarms per minute should occur. Your SCADA installation requires an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. In this case fewer alarms are more effective as the human mind can only focus on a few things at a time. Adroit can help you to achieve this alarming system as follows: - The AlarmManagement agent can help you by generating statistics from the data produced by the alarming system. This allows you to have efficient and meaningful incident reviews to identify and remove nuisance alarms by analysing the counts, frequencies, durations and acknowledgement times of incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). . Note: By repeating this process regularly, you will be able to ensure that only relevant alarms are generated thereby improving your alarming system. - Adroit has improved the legacy alarming system, to allow you to assign a priority PER ALARM (previously priorities could only be assigned PER AGENT), which allows your operators to filter out lower priority alarms, if required. Quick Start to Configure and Record Incidents (Alarms/Events) . For details on how to prioritise your alarms into categories of importance, see Configuring Incident (Alarm) Priorities . For further details about alarm management, read the ISA SP18.02 Alarm Management Standard. -->

In the past alarms were hardwired into the panels, which limited their number; now that alarms are software-driven, means that you can have an unlimited number of alarms.

Title: Why is alarm management needed?
In the past alarms were hardwired into the panels, which limited their number; now that alarms are software-driven, means that you can have an unlimited number of alarms. In an effort to keep the operators sufficiently informed, SCADA installations typically use lots of alarms, each of which usually have very little awareness of the other alarms in the system. This means that each incident can generate a flood of alarms, which causes operators to become overloaded and confused and as a result they may even start ignoring alarms! Therefore LESS alarms are MORE effective. Alarm management is concerned with improving the QUALITY of the information within the alarming configuration. This information should be used to reduce the QUANTITY of nuisance alarms (red herrings) so that only the most important and relevant alarms are displayed for your process. In other words alarm management counteracts inefficient alarming by allowing you to create an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. The following procedure describes the recommended method of using the AlarmManagement agent to configure and record your active incidents so that you can analyse this information to improve your alarming configuration.

In Adroit, Alarm agents can monitor other agents for preset conditions or states.

Title: What is an incident?
Steps:
In Adroit, Alarm agents can monitor other agents for preset conditions or states. So that when a monitored condition occurs in an agent its Alarm agent uses predefined reporting methods to alert the necessary people and/or applications. That is why Alarming in Adroit primarily involves the configuration of the following two things: - The preset conditions or states of each agent that you need to alarm, known as alarm types, which each constitute a separate alarm or event. - The alarm routes that specify which alarm destinations (reporting mechanisms) you need to use to communicate the generated alarms and events to the necessary personnel and/or applications. In Adroit an incident occurs when an agent enters a condition defined by an alarm type that is being monitored by an Alarm agent. However, an incident is ONLY an alarm, if it needs to be responded to; otherwise it is an event. -->

About Alarm Routes Top About Alarm Routes An alarm route simply tells the Alarm agent how it must deal with active incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type.

Title: About Alarm Routes
About Alarm Routes Top About Alarm Routes An alarm route simply tells the Alarm agent how it must deal with active incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). . In other words it specifies which reporting mechanisms (output destinations) this incident must use to effectively notify the relevant plant personnel and/or applications of its occurrence. An Alarm agent can use one or more alarm routes to specify which alarm destinations to send the active incidents of the agents that it is monitoring. Where each route in an Alarm agent consists of two following elements: Best Practice: Always alarm agents from route 2 onwards never use routes 0 and 1. These routes are used internally by Adroit for reporting the system alarms and events. - A route number, starting from 0. For details about and the recommended usage of the 4 alarm routes provided by the defaultAlarmAgent, see About the defaultAlarmAgent . To add a route to an Alarm agent: - Edit the required Alarm agent. - Select the Routes tab from the Edit Alarm Agent dialog. - Click the Add Route button to create a new route for this Alarm agent - Specify the required destination/s for incidents that use this alarm route. To use an existing route of an Alarm agent: - Edit the required Alarm agent. - Select the Routes tab from the Edit Alarm Agent dialog. - Select the existing route number, from the Select route number list box. - Specify the required destination/s for incidents that use this alarm route. To remove a route from an Alarm agent: - Edit the required Alarm agent. - Select the Routes tab from the Edit Alarm Agent dialog. - Select the required route number, from the Select route number list box. - Click the Remove Route button. Note: You can ONLY remove a route if NO alarm types have selected this route number. Otherwise a “Couldn’t delete routing message box is displayed. - One or more route destinations (options) to report the incidents that are communicated via this route to the necessary personnel and/or applications. Click for more details: So if an alarm or event is assigned to a specific Route, it is automatically sent to ALL the destinations that are configured on this alarm Route.

These alarm destinations are grouped into the following 4 main categories: Note: Each destination is typically managed by a specific agent type.

Title: About Alarm Routes
These alarm destinations are grouped into the following 4 main categories: Note: Each destination is typically managed by a specific agent type. The following two categories are specific to individual Alarm agents: Alarm Lists: The AlarmList agent, allows you to separate or combine your active incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). and/or to LOCALLY acknowledged them from one or more Alarm windows. Note: You CANNOT locally acknowledge the active alarms listed by an Alarm agent. Audio Devices: - The Beeper agent, which provides simple audio output using the built-in computer loudspeaker. - The MultiMedia agent launches a Windows compatible multimedia file, such as .WAV, .MID, .AVI or .RMI The following two categories apply to ALL Alarm agents: Outputs: - The AlarmManagement agent, which collects and if necessary, configure incidents from one or more alarm agents and sends them to an OLE DB compatible database, so they can be analysed to improve your alarm system. - The EventOutput agent, which can print incidents locally or remotely; save them to a .CSV file and if necessary, log them to an OLE DB compatible database for reporting and/or analysis purposes. - The Notify agent, which can transmit incidents via SMS Short Message Service is a service (protocol) for sending short text messages to and from mobile phones. or a paging service direct to a designated person. This can inform off site personal of unacknowledged alarms and if necessary of process values and operator messages. Event Logs: The EventLogging agent, which can log incidents to the Windows Application event log on a specific computer and/or to an OLE DB database for reporting and/or analysis purposes. Note1: Each route can use different output devices or share the same output devices with other routes. Note2: You can specify a different alarm route for each alarm type of the monitored agent. These alarm destinations are classified according to their scope, as follows: - LOCAL destinations, which are specific to the Alarm agent that is being used and so apply to all the agents that are being alarmed by this agent or - GLOBAL destinations, which common to ALL Alarm agents and so apply to ALL agents that being alarmed in this Adroit installation.

Local Incident Destinations : to select and manage incident reporting options SPECIFIC to each Alarm agents.

Title: About Alarm Routes
Local Incident Destinations : to select and manage incident reporting options SPECIFIC to each Alarm agents. Global Incident Destinations : to select and manage incident reporting options COMMON to all Alarm agents. Therefore, if your strategy involves using different Alarm agents to split other various sections of our plant up, these routes will be different but end in the same destinations e.g. same alarm list -->

Audio Devices: - The Beeper agent, which provides simple audio output using the built-in computer loudspeaker. - The MultiMedia agent launches a Windows compatible multimedia file, such as .WAV, .MID, .AVI or .RMI The following two categories apply to ALL Alarm agents: Outputs: - The AlarmManagement agent, which collects and if necessary, configure incidents from one or more alarm agents and sends them to an OLE DB compatible database, so they can be analysed to improve your alarm system. - The EventOutput agent, which can print incidents locally or remotely; save them to a .CSV file and if necessary, log them to an OLE DB compatible database for reporting and/or analysis purposes. - The Notify agent, which can transmit incidents via SMS Short Message Service is a service (protocol) for sending short text messages to and from mobile phones. or a paging service direct to a designated person. This can inform off site personal of unacknowledged alarms and if necessary of process values and operator messages. Event Logs: The EventLogging agent, which can log incidents to the Windows Application event log on a specific computer and/or to an OLE DB database for reporting and/or analysis purposes. Note1: Each route can use different output devices or share the same output devices with other routes. Note2: You can specify a different alarm route for each alarm type of the monitored agent. These alarm destinations are classified according to their scope, as follows: - LOCAL destinations, which are specific to the Alarm agent that is being used and so apply to all the agents that are being alarmed by this agent or - GLOBAL destinations, which common to ALL Alarm agents and so apply to ALL agents that being alarmed in this Adroit installation.

Local Incident Destinations : to select and manage incident reporting options SPECIFIC to each Alarm agents.

Title: About Alarm Routes
Local Incident Destinations : to select and manage incident reporting options SPECIFIC to each Alarm agents. Global Incident Destinations : to select and manage incident reporting options COMMON to all Alarm agents. Therefore, if your strategy involves using different Alarm agents to split other various sections of our plant up, these routes will be different but end in the same destinations e.g. same alarm list -->

About Alarm Types Top About Alarm Types An alarm type is simply the required condition or state of an agent that you need to alarm.

Title: About Alarm Types
About Alarm Types Top About Alarm Types An alarm type is simply the required condition or state of an agent that you need to alarm. This can also contain a list of slots of this agent, which are reported when the alarm occurs. In Adroit , each agent drives the following status bits: These status bits are divided into the following categories: - Common Status Bits , which indicate their internal status (or integrity) and are common to all agents. For instance, these can indicate failures within the Adroit system itself. - Specific Status Bits , which indicate the status of the values driven by or contained in the agent and are specific to each agent type. For instance, these can indicate plant upsets or process variable excursions. Each alarm type requires two of the following three components: - specify which of these status bits must be simultaneously enabled or disabled and - provide a descriptive name for the specified condition, this usually takes the form of a descriptive abbreviation. For instance "Overheating" for an Analog agent type or "Tripped" for a Digital agent type. - if necessary, specify which slots of the agent should be reported when the specified condition occurs, in other words ONLY select those slots that will help clarify or troubleshoot this state of the agent. For instance: To create an alarm type : You can either create alarm types from the Alarm agent for ALL agent types or from the Alarming dialog for the agent type of the specific agent that you are alarming. To edit an alarm type :You can either edit alarm types from the Alarm agent for ALL agent types or from the Alarming dialog for the agent type of the specific agent that you are alarming. To remove an alarm type : You can ONLY remove alarm types from the Alarm agent for ALL agent types. When you ‘alarm’ an agent, you simply select the required alarm type/s that the specified Alarm agent should monitor for this agent. Then when the necessary status bit/s are set in this agent that match one of the selected Agent Types, the Alarm agent communicates incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). via the selected alarm route. Example: By default each agent type provides one or more pre-configured alarm types. This means that one set of alarm types will be created for Analog agents and another set for Digital agents. If necessary, you can create your own agent types. Although it is NOT recommended that you modify the predefined alarm types. Note: Alarm types are specified per agent type; therefore once you have created the required agent type for one agent it is available for ALL agents of this type. The default alarm types are pre-configured in the postload Adroit database file . For further details of this file, see About the Postload Database File . -->

About Backup Procedures Top About Backup Procedures It is important to create a backup procedure to guarantee disaster avoidance rather than just disaster recovery and also to provide an easy way for transferring an Adroit project or system to another computer.

Title: About Backup Procedures
Steps:
About Backup Procedures Top About Backup Procedures It is important to create a backup procedure to guarantee disaster avoidance rather than just disaster recovery and also to provide an easy way for transferring an Adroit project or system to another computer. Hence, this backup procedure should include all the files utilised during plant operation and include storage facilities as well as locations, since critical data should be stored in an alternative location, such as a drive or remote hard disk etc. For these reasons it is recommended to use the System Backup and Restore facility provided by the Adroit Config Editor utility to execute and manage such a backup procedure. For details, see System Backup and Restore . Note: This requires you to have installed SmartUI . The backup process generates a single compressed file in the specified location, which contains the date and time of its creation, which contains all the relevant registry settings and all the files and folders containing the user-configuration of the currently specified Configuration. When restoring, you can restore between x86 and x64 operating system architectures and across different operating system language sets. However, any file paths within the agent database (.wgp) file are not currently converted and still need to be manually edited after restoring the project. This backup includes the following files and settings: - Adroit data files . This will backup up the files required by your Adroit projects, where multiple file locations can be specified. WGP files, provide two features to assist with their regular backup. For details, see Backing Up Adroit Database (.WGP) Files . WARNING! These features are merely intended to AUGMENT the existing backup system and NOT to REPLACE it i.e. it is still imperative that an efficient backup system is in place! - Event Logs . This will ONLY export the application; security and system event logs files. These event log files CANNOT be restored but can be viewed by using the Event Viewer. - Adroit registry. This will backup both the global Adroit registry settings and the Adroit registry settings specific to the current user. This will contain the Adroit configuration, workspaces and Adroit protocol driver configuration settings. -->

The following Behaviours can be added to controls and/or graphic elements (vectors): Tip: You can use the Behaviours tab of the SmartUI Designer ribbon to add, edit or remove these Behaviours and in some cases the Child Behaviour option.

Title: Available Behaviours
The following Behaviours can be added to controls and/or graphic elements (vectors): Tip: You can use the Behaviours tab of the SmartUI Designer ribbon to add, edit or remove these Behaviours and in some cases the Child Behaviour option. For details, see Child Behaviours . - Bind Value : to drive a data element (value) to and/or from the value of a property of a control or vector. - Color : to assign colors to the two states of a digital (Boolean) value; to blink a specific color property or the VISIBILITY property either continuously or triggered by a value. You can also define states of color based on specific value ranges to provide a visual indication of a value. You can also define states of color based on a bit mask - a specific sequence of bits that are set (to 1) for up to 32 bits to provide a visual indication of each bit mask. - Display Value : to display and if necessary format a value. - Execute Command : to perform commands, such as launching an application or opening, closing or printing a graphic form or logging a user on or off and/or switching users. - Flip Bitmap : to create a defined sequence of images or a multi-image display, which can only be added to a Picture vector. - Location : to dynamically move the object linearly in a defined X-Y direction by means of a monitored value. - Operator Action : typically provides methods that allow end users to change a value at runtime. - Percentage Fill : to dynamically fill the object by means of a monitored value. - Rotation : to dynamically rotate the object by means of a monitored value. - size : to dynamically resize the object linearly by means of a monitored value. - Tooltip : to display additional information usually concerning this object when the mouse cursor (pointer) hovers also called a mouse hover, is the action of putting the mouse cursor (pointer) over a designated area. over it. - Visibility : to display or hide this object depending on a value. Note: The behaviour configuration dialogs typically provide an Advanced View button that displays more advanced configuration options. Tip: Use the Copy with Behaviours right click option or the SHIFT+CTRL+C shortcut to copy a control or graphic element AND its added Behaviours and then paste it as usual. Tip1: When adding a Behaviour to a SmartUI Template A graphic form that has one or more configured aliases and is therefore designed to be displayed within a TemplateGO control. , you can use {} notation to automatically create an alias for any data element field. For more details, see Working with SmartUI Templates . Tip2: When adding a Behaviour to a wizard A pre-drawn and/or pre-configured skeleton of graphical objects and their assigned Behaviours (if any), which has placeholders (substitutions) for data elements. , you can use {} notation to automatically create a substitution for any data element field. For more details, see Working with wizards . To add a Behaviour to a control or graphic element: Ensure that you have added the required control or graphic element to the graphic form. - Select the required control or graphic element. - If necessary, select the Behaviours tab from the SmartUI Designer ribbon. Note: Any Behaviour that cannot be applied to this control or graphic element will be greyed out. - Select the required Behaviour from the relevant group. Tip: You can also select its glyph to display its task menu and then select the required Behaviour from the New Behaviour drop down list. This displays the configuration dialog of this Behaviour.

Tip: When you add or edit a Behaviour you can name it, which makes it easier to identify the spiders and their regions associated with your Behaviours.

Title: Available Behaviours
Tip: When you add or edit a Behaviour you can name it, which makes it easier to identify the spiders and their regions associated with your Behaviours. To edit a Behaviour of a control or graphic element: - Right click the required control or graphic element to the graphic form. - Select the required BehaviourName# menu item, where BehaviourName is the name of the added Behaviour and # usually only appears if more than one of same type of Behaviours have been added. For example: Execute Command1 Tip: You can also select its glyph to display its task menu and then select the required link beneath the Behaviours heading. This displays the configuration dialog of this Behaviour. Tip: The Behaviours tab of the SmartUI Designer ribbon provides the Edit Behaviour list box that lists all the Behaviours configured for the currently selected form component. Clicking its browse button displays the configuration dialog of the currently selected behaviour. To remove one or more added Behaviours from a control or graphic element: - Select the required control or graphic element. - If necessary, select the Behaviours tab from the SmartUI Designer ribbon. - Select the Remove command from the Remove group. Tip: You can also select its glyph to display its task menu and then select the Remove link beneath the Behaviours heading. This displays the Behaviour Removal configuration dialog. - Select (check the checkboxes) of the Behaviour/s that you want to remove from this list in the Behaviour Removal configuration dialog. WARNING! Ensure that ONLY the Behaviour/s you do not require is selected, since no deletion confirmation dialogs are displayed. - Click the Finish button to remove the selected Behaviour/s or Cancel to abort. -->

About connection communication methods About connection communication methods The purpose of creating a connection is to transfer data between the Smart UI Client refers to either the Designer or the Operator, both of which are client applications of the Server.

Title: About connection communication methods
About connection communication methods About connection communication methods The purpose of creating a connection is to transfer data between the Smart UI Client refers to either the Designer or the Operator, both of which are client applications of the Server. and Smart UI Server computer, using one of the following methods: Click for more detailed descriptions: Note: The available method(s) depends upon the specified connection Type or how the two computers are physically connected. - Subscribe: This is a push-based communication method in which the Smart UI Client waits for the data that has changed to be pushed, or sent to it. In this case the Smart UI Client never looks for new data, it always uses data pushed from the Smart UI Server. Note1: There is no subscription period, data is pushed to the Client whenever it is requested or changed. Note2: The Internet connection type does not support this since the Internet is by definition a pull-based communication network. Tip: This is recommended communication method when using the Local Area Network connection type, since it is the fastest and most precise method. Comparative example: The following is what the Smart UI Client would receive when using the Subscribe communication method to retrieve a sinusoidal curve, whose data changes every second: - Poll: This is a pull-based communication method in which the Smart UI Client can pull information from the Smart UI Server by checking it periodically and retrieving any new or updated data that it finds. In this case data is never sent to the Smart UI Client from the Smart UI Server. Note: The ClientPollTime setting of the Client specifies the time interval used to pull data from the Server. For details on accessing this setting, see Advanced Designer settings or Advanced Operator settings as applicable. Tip: This communication process is provided specifically for the Internet connection type. The following two types of polling are supported: - Poll (Send all values): The Smart UI Client will fetch all the values that have changed since the time of the last polling period. Note: This is the most precise of the two polling types, although requires a sizable bandwidth. Comparative example: The following is what the Client would receive when using the Poll (Send all values) communication method to retrieve a sinusoidal curve, whose data changes every second, when using a polling interval of 10 seconds: - Poll (Send most recent values): The Smart UI Client will only fetch the most recent value at the time of the polling period. Note: This is the least precise communication method of the three and should only be used if you have limited bandwidth or do not want to send a large amount of data over the Internet. Comparative example: The following is what the Client would receive when using the Poll (Send most recent values) communication method to retrieve a sinusoidal curve, whose data changes every second, when using a polling interval of 10 seconds: Note: The bandwidth requirements for a connection depends upon a number of factors, such as the update requirements and the size of the graphic forms. So keep the graphic form sizes small; for example use JPG files instead of BMP files. -->

About CSV Connectors Top About CSV Connectors CSV Connectors are complex Connectors, in that they are not device-specific but instead can globally configure agents and can create a fully configured Adroit agent database (.WGP file).

Title: About CSV Connectors
About CSV Connectors Top About CSV Connectors CSV Connectors are complex Connectors, in that they are not device-specific but instead can globally configure agents and can create a fully configured Adroit agent database (.WGP file). Each CSV Connector Link creates four CSV files that can be configured to provide the information necessary to configure a WGP file. Each of these files can create agents and are located in the CSV subfolder of the designated project folder, which is typically C:\ProgramData\Adroit Technologies\Adroit\Configurations\Default \CSV. Link configuration: This Connector does NOT provide a Link configuration dialog. Since the four CSV filenames automatically use the name of the Link , as follows: If the Link name is AS1 then the associated CSV filenames are: - AS1.agents.csv: the agent definition file (see below) - AS1.scanning.csv: the scanning definition file (see below) - AS1.alarming.csv: the alarming definition file (see below) - AS1.logging.csv: the logging definition file (see below) Template implementation: Specify the applicable template names in the designated columns within the four CSV files. The agent definition file: This file should ONLY contain those agents that have not been alarmed, scanned or logged. Each agent is specified by the following 4 columns: Note : ONLY the first TWO columns are REQUIRED. - Agent Name : The name of the agent that you want to create. For instance, ANA001 or DIG001. Note : Please ensure that you adhere to the Adroit agent naming conventions when specifying this name. - Agent Type : The type or category of this Agent Name, most often this corresponds to the required data type, such as Analog or Digital although this can specify a more complex agent such as Counter or Expression etc. - Agent Template : If necessary, specify the name of the agent creation template that customises the default values (slots) of this Agent Type . - Description : If necessary, specify a brief description of the intended purpose of the Agent Name, which is purely for information purposes. Note : This file does not need to contain any agents that are defined in any of the other scanning, alarming or logging definition files. The scanning definition file: This file should contain all your process values that you want to configure for scanning the process of communicating a value (slot), typically to and/or from a front-end device (FED). .

Each process value that you want to communicate is specified by the following 11 columns: - Agent : The name of the agent that you want to scan.

Title: About CSV Connectors
Each process value that you want to communicate is specified by the following 11 columns: - Agent : The name of the agent that you want to scan. For instance, ANA001 or DIG001. Note: Please ensure that you adhere to the Adroit agent naming conventions when specifying this name. - Agent Type : The type or category of this Agent , most often this corresponds to the required data type, such as Analog or Digital although this can specify a more complex agent such as Counter or Expression etc. - Agent Template : If necessary, specify the name of the agent creation template that customises the default values (slots) of this Agent Type . - Device : The name of the device, configured in Adroit Setup (PSEXE) that communicates to the required FED front-end device, which is a device that is accessed directly by the user, such as a PLC or RTU. . - Slot : The name of the slot a value (attribute) or field within an agent that can be retrieved and/or set. of this Agent that you want to scan. - Address : The address within the FED (Device) that this Slot (value) should be communicated to/from. - Rate (msecs) : The time, in milliseconds, which will elapse before this value is communicated to or from this Device . - Deadband : The deadband limit for this value. Any CHANGE in value LESS than this deadband limit will NOT be communicated. - Output (0/1 ): To enable or disable the output enable setting for this scanned value. If enabled (1) then this value can be written to this Device (FED). Note: This setting does not prevent this value from being updated by the FED. - Inhibit (0/1) : To enable or disable the scan inhibit setting for this scanned value. If enabled (1) then this value CANNOT be changed by this Device (FED). Note: This setting does not prevent this value from changing the value in the FED. - Template : If necessary, specify the name of the scanning template that customises the default values for the following columns of this file: Slot , Rate (msecs) , Deadband , Output (0/1) and/or Inhibit (0/1) and can ALSO specify a scanning suffix for the Address . Note : If you are using a template, then ONLY specify these columns if they DIFFER from the default values provided by this template.

The alarming definition file: This file should contain all your process values that you typically want to alarm the process of monitoring an agent for the occurrence of a specific abnormal condition or state (alarm type).

Title: About CSV Connectors
The alarming definition file: This file should contain all your process values that you typically want to alarm the process of monitoring an agent for the occurrence of a specific abnormal condition or state (alarm type). . Each alarm type a named (abnormal) condition or state of an agent that is defined by which of its status bits are simultaneously ON or OFF, which can also list the slots of this agent to report when this condition occurs. required by a process value is typically specified by the following 8 columns: - Agent : The name of the agent that you want to alarm. For instance, ANA001 or DIG001. Title: The main difference between a Select query and a DataBinder
Although this seems similar to the function performed by a Select query, the main difference between a query and DataBinder is that: - Select queries (and the queries in previous versions) only return static snapshots of the selected data that are only current at the time at which the query is performed. - DataBinders remain in constant communication with the database and so can provide a ‘live’ view of your data, if necessary. This makes it possible for DataBinders to modify the data within the database, so that instead of merely viewing the existing records, additional records can be added or existing records can be removed. Click for more details: To access the data within a DataBinder, create a graphic form and add a VIZNETDataBinder component. This launches a configuration dialog to select the required DataBinder and which of its tables and their fields to display on this graphic form. The controls and components to view and/or modify the selected fields for each of the selected tables can be automatically generated and added to this graphic form. Note: Please ensure that the DataBinder contains all the primary key A primary key is one or more fields in the table of a database that uniquely identify each record stored in this, so they can locate records. Therefore, the primary key column/s must have unique values for each their rows. column/s for a table, if you require your users to add or remove records from this table. These primary key column/s, however, do not need to be displayed on the graphic form. More advanced users can: - Add additional controls to this graphic form and link them to the required database fields by binding the required BindingSource component to their DataBinding property. - Configure the DataBinder control to specify which controls will be used to provide the values of any parameters. - Configure the DataBinder control to specify the maximum number of records to be retrieved from the database. - Report the data within a DataBinder using a charting control. Typically one would use a Bar, Column or Pie charting control. - Configure the navigator controls to determine which functions are available to a specified user.

About datasources and data elements Top About datasources and data elements The SmartUI Server is a "data portal" which integrates data from a number of disparate sources.

Title: About datasources and data elements
About datasources and data elements Top About datasources and data elements The SmartUI Server is a "data portal" which integrates data from a number of disparate sources. Each source of data requires a datasource plugin before it can be associated with the SmartUI Server. This provides the ability to expose its data as data elements to the Server and, if necessary, provides special functions or methods to further interact with its data. Click for more details: For instance, the OLEDB datasource plugin exposes data within OLEDB databases to the Server as data elements. While the datasource plugin behaves as a datasource template, it is the datasource itself, which is the actual connection to each source of data wherever it is physically located. By using its datasource plugin, the datasource is able to expose the connected data to the Server as data elements. It also provides any special functions so that users can further interact with this connected data. For instance, an OLEDB datasource connects to an OLEDB database (e.g. Database1.mdb), by using the OLEDB datasource plugin to expose the tables and fields within this database as data elements to the Server. A data element is essentially a finite component of data contained within a datasource that behaves in a generic manner. In other words, although data elements may contain disparate data, they all possess generic attributes so that they can be similarly interacted and worked with. For instance, a data element would be a specific field within an OLEDB datasource e.g. Database1.mdb. Note1: In addition to making its data available as data elements, a datasource plugin may also or may only provide additional functionality for interacting with each datasource and/or its data, known as special functions. Note2: Each data element contains a number of internal properties, one of which monitors the status of the veracity or accuracy of its data. If this is set to anything other than GOOD, then any controls that displays this data element in a graphic form will become disabled (greyed out). For details on associating data elements with controls, see Animating graphic forms . Note3: Access to data elements and special functions need to be controlled separately for each datasource that is created. For details, see Working with data element security or Working with special function security .

Generally speaking, the SmartUI Server connects to data using two different types of datasources, which are distinguished by the relation of the data to the SmartUI Server, itself, as follows: - External datasources that link to data from the outside world, for instance, the OLEDB datasource.

Title: About datasources and data elements
Generally speaking, the SmartUI Server connects to data using two different types of datasources, which are distinguished by the relation of the data to the SmartUI Server, itself, as follows: - External datasources that link to data from the outside world, for instance, the OLEDB datasource. Note: This datasource plugin only has one datasource per Server, called Profile . About Filtering Prioritised Incidents Top About Filtering Prioritised Incidents One way to ensure that your operators ONLY receive IMPORTANT alarms is to prioritise your alarms into categories of importance.

Title: About Filtering Prioritised Incidents
About Filtering Prioritised Incidents Top About Filtering Prioritised Incidents One way to ensure that your operators ONLY receive IMPORTANT alarms is to prioritise your alarms into categories of importance. Since some alarms are critical, whereas others are more informational in nature. Once you have prioritised your incidents, Adroit provides the following ways to filter your incidents, based on their priority: - You can configure the priority level of each Alarm agent to discard any alarm that has a LOWER priority level. In this way you can to filter out the alarms of less important or less critical agents. WARNING! This method REMOVES the lower prioritised alarms so that they are NOT REPORTED. This method should ONLY be used during times of process upheaval or when alarm flooding occurs (this is indicative of a badly configured alarm configuration). To set the alarm priority filter of an Alarm Agent: Any incident that has a LOWER priority is DISCARDED by the Alarm agent and is as if this alarm did not exist at all. - Edit the required Alarm agent. - Select the General tab from the Edit Alarm Agent dialog. - Specify the LOWEST incident priority level in the Priority Filter edit box of the General dialog as follows: 0: lowest 1: low 2: normal 3: high 4: highest The default is 0, which means that ALL alarms are dealt with. - Click the OK button. Note: The EventLogging agent can also EXCLUDE events from agents based on their configured Alarm Priority. - You can let your Alarm agents process ALL the active incidents (their default setting) and then use the priorities of the incidents to filter out the unnecessary incidents. For instance the Alarm List Viewer windows are able to filter incidents by specifying the required range of priorities. For details, see Row Filtering Configuration for Alarm Windows. Note: Adroit also provides the Filter Group setting, which is specified in the header of each agent and is typically used to denote different plant areas, so that the alarms can be filtered per plant area. For details on how to prioritise your alarms into categories of importance, see Configuring Incident (Alarm) Priorities . -->

About Power Factor Top About Power Factor The importance of the power factor lies in the fact that electricity providers supply customers with volt-amperes, but bill them for watts.

Title: About Power Factor
About Power Factor Top About Power Factor The importance of the power factor lies in the fact that electricity providers supply customers with volt-amperes, but bill them for watts. Power factors below 1.0 require an electricity provider to generate more than the minimum volt-amperes necessary to supply the real power (watts). Since this increases the electricity provider’s generation and transmission costs, they may charge additional costs to customers who have a power factor below some limit. In other words, most electric billing is done in kilowatt-hours, which is determined by the following equation: Kilowatt-hours = (Volts * Amperes) * power factor * run time If we assume that the run time, volts, and kilowatt-hours are constant, then as the power factor decreases the amperage must rise to compensate. The converse is also true, if the power factor is raised for a load, then the amperage is reduced. For this reason, by adjusting the power factor of a system to very near unity, you ONLY pay for the power that you use. A good power factor is considered to be greater than 0.85. To understand the power factor is more detail, it is necessary to know that the following three types of power are used to describe energy flow in an alternating current (A.C.) electrical system: - Real power is the actual power that is being used or the ability of the system to perform work and is measured in watts (kW). - Apparent power is the power that the system seems to be using, being the product of the current and voltage of the circuit and is therefore measured in volt-amperes (kVA). - Reactive power is ‘invisible’ or wattless power, in which energy stored in the load is returned to the source and is measured in kVAR, which stands for volt-amperes-reactive. The power factor of an alternating current (A.C.) electrical system is simply the ratio of the real power to the apparent power and is a number between 0 and 1. The following ‘power triangle’ describes the relationship between these three types of power: Therefore, from this power triangle the following can be seen: - When there is no reactive power element, such as for a purely resistive load (i.e. heating elements, incandescent lighting, etc.) then the actual and the apparent power are the same i.e.

there is no reactive power and so the power factor is 1.

Title: About Power Factor
there is no reactive power and so the power factor is 1. - When a reactive power element exists then the apparent power can be greater than the real power component, which decreases the power factor. This reactive power element can be generated by: - Inductive loads such as transformers and motors (any type of wound coil) generate reactive power with current waveform lagging the voltage - Capacitive loads such as capacitor banks or buried cable generate reactive power with current phase leading the voltage. It is often possible to adjust the power factor of a system to very near unity. This practice is known as power factor correction and is achieved by switching in or out banks of inductors or capacitors. About Power Factor Top About Power Factor The importance of the power factor lies in the fact that electricity providers supply customers with volt-amperes, but bill them for watts.

Title: About Power Factor
About Power Factor Top About Power Factor The importance of the power factor lies in the fact that electricity providers supply customers with volt-amperes, but bill them for watts. Power factors below 1.0 require an electricity provider to generate more than the minimum volt-amperes necessary to supply the real power (watts). Since this increases the electricity provider’s generation and transmission costs, they may charge additional costs to customers who have a power factor below some limit. In other words, most electric billing is done in kilowatt-hours, which is determined by the following equation: Kilowatt-hours = (Volts * Amperes) * power factor * run time If we assume that the run time, volts, and kilowatt-hours are constant, then as the power factor decreases the amperage must rise to compensate. The converse is also true, if the power factor is raised for a load, then the amperage is reduced. For this reason, by adjusting the power factor of a system to very near unity, you ONLY pay for the power that you use. A good power factor is considered to be greater than 0.85. To understand the power factor is more detail, it is necessary to know that the following three types of power are used to describe energy flow in an alternating current (A.C.) electrical system: - Real power is the actual power that is being used or the ability of the system to perform work and is measured in watts (kW). - Apparent power is the power that the system seems to be using, being the product of the current and voltage of the circuit and is therefore measured in volt-amperes (kVA). - Reactive power is ‘invisible’ or wattless power, in which energy stored in the load is returned to the source and is measured in kVAR, which stands for volt-amperes-reactive. The power factor of an alternating current (A.C.) electrical system is simply the ratio of the real power to the apparent power and is a number between 0 and 1. The following ‘power triangle’ describes the relationship between these three types of power: Therefore, from this power triangle the following can be seen: - When there is no reactive power element, such as for a purely resistive load (i.e. heating elements, incandescent lighting, etc.) then the actual and the apparent power are the same i.e.

there is no reactive power and so the power factor is 1.

Title: About Power Factor
there is no reactive power and so the power factor is 1. - When a reactive power element exists then the apparent power can be greater than the real power component, which decreases the power factor. This reactive power element can be generated by: - Inductive loads such as transformers and motors (any type of wound coil) generate reactive power with current waveform lagging the voltage - Capacitive loads such as capacitor banks or buried cable generate reactive power with current phase leading the voltage. It is often possible to adjust the power factor of a system to very near unity. This practice is known as power factor correction and is achieved by switching in or out banks of inductors or capacitors. For example the inductive effect of motor loads may be offset by locally connected capacitors and vice verse.
